case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a party that failed to raise a statutory-interpretation argument in the district court (or properly on appeal) may nevertheless obtain reversal based on that new legal theory, and what standard governs a federal court of appeals’ discretion to consider such a forfeited argument.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal appellate preservation/forfeiture doctrine (judge-made), including standards governing consideration of forfeited issues on appeal; potentially intersecting with Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 52/46 and Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 28 (briefing requirements), but the core dispute concerns the Tenth Circuit’s discretionary forfeiture standards rather than a single substantive statute.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Flowers Foods, Inc., et al.) argue that the Tenth Circuit applied an overly strict approach to forfeiture by refusing to consider a newly presented legal argument even though it involves a pure question of law; they contend appellate courts should more readily address purely legal, outcome-determinative issues to reach the correct result, particularly where the record is adequate and the issue’s resolution is clear, and that the Tenth Circuit’s 'beyond reasonable doubt' framing improperly limits appellate discretion and entrenches erroneous judgments.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Angelo Brock) argues that the forfeiture rules are essential to fair, orderly adjudication and adversarial testing, and that the Tenth Circuit properly declined to entertain petitioners’ new legal theory because it was not preserved and its correct resolution was not so certain as to justify bypassing preservation; respondent emphasizes that even 'pure law' exceptions are narrow, that allowing late-arising theories would prejudice litigants and encourage sandbagging, and that the Tenth Circuit’s standard (requiring certainty before excusing forfeiture) is a permissible exercise of appellate discretion.

John Roberts.reasoning: The petitioners’ strongest point—that a “pure” statutory-interpretation question should be reached to avoid an erroneous judgment—still does not overcome Singleton v. Wulff’s baseline that entertaining issues not pressed or passed upon below is discretionary and ordinarily inappropriate, especially where adversarial development may have been different. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Hormel is helpful, but it cuts against petitioners: Hormel recognizes only narrow, prudential exceptions keyed to an adequate record and avoidance of injustice, not an entitlement to reversal on a late-raised theory. Justice Kagan’s administrability point reinforces my minimalist concern for legitimacy: channeling discretion through a high-certainty screen deters sandbagging and preserves the district court’s role without foreclosing truly exceptional cases. On this record, where the statutory question is not shown to be outcome-determinative and certain, I would not disturb the court of appeals’ enforcement of forfeiture.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest contention—that a court of appeals must reach a forfeited but “purely legal” statutory argument to avoid an erroneous judgment—finds no footing in constitutional or statutory text, and our precedents treat it as discretionary at most. As the Chief Justice explains, Singleton v. Wulff makes consideration of issues not pressed or passed upon below “ordinarily” inappropriate and leaves the matter to appellate discretion, which undermines any claimed entitlement to reversal. Justice Kavanaugh’s discussion of Hormel confirms that the exception is prudential and narrow, turning on adequacy of the record and avoidance of injustice, not a categorical rule whenever an argument is legal in character. Given that framework, the Tenth Circuit’s “beyond reasonable doubt/certainty” screen is a permissible method of exercising discretion consistent with ordinary preservation principles and does not conflict with any binding text or precedent.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioners’ strongest point remains that a forfeited “pure question of law” should be corrected on appeal to avoid an unlawful judgment, but that argument overreads our cases and would convert a narrow safety valve into an entitlement. As the Chief Justice emphasizes, Singleton v. Wulff treats consideration of issues not pressed or passed upon below as discretionary and ordinarily inappropriate, particularly where the record and adversarial presentation may have been shaped by the parties’ earlier theory and the correct answer is not “certain” on this record. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Hormel v. Helvering reinforces that any exception is prudential and fact-sensitive (adequate record, fairness, necessity to prevent injustice), not a categorical requirement keyed solely to the “legal” label. Given the practical consequences—inviting sandbagging and undermining orderly procedure—the Tenth Circuit’s high-certainty screen is a permissible way to channel discretion rather than an abuse of it.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioners’ strongest point—that courts of appeals should reach a forfeited statutory-interpretation argument whenever it is “purely legal”—still overreads our cases: Singleton v. Wulff makes clear this is discretionary and turns on fairness, prejudice, and whether the issue benefited from adversarial testing. Chief Justice Roberts’ emphasis on institutional legitimacy and the way a late shift can distort how the record and briefing were developed tracks my pragmatic concern for litigants (often less resourced) who reasonably litigate the case as framed below and would be disadvantaged by appellate sandbagging. Justice Kagan’s defense of the Tenth Circuit’s “certainty/beyond reasonable doubt” screen persuades me it is an administrable, deterrence-oriented way to channel discretion without foreclosing relief in the truly exceptional case. Hormel, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, supports narrow equitable exceptions but does not create an entitlement to reversal on a new theory, so nothing here undermines enforcing forfeiture on this record.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point remains that a court of appeals should correct a forfeited but purely legal statutory-interpretation error to avoid cementing a wrong rule of federal law. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, Singleton v. Wulff makes that sort of review discretionary and “ordinarily” inappropriate where adversarial testing and record development may have been shaped by the parties’ earlier theory; nothing in Singleton creates a duty to reach every late-raised legal contention. Justice Kavanaugh’s invocation of Hormel reinforces that exceptions turn on adequacy of the record and fairness (including prejudice and sandbagging concerns), not on the mere label “pure law,” and the Tenth Circuit’s “certainty/beyond reasonable doubt” screen is a pragmatic way to channel that discretion rather than a departure from it. Because the asserted statutory meaning is not shown to be indisputable on this record and could have affected how the case was litigated below, I do not see a legal basis to disturb the court of appeals’ enforcement of forfeiture.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest point is that a purely legal, statutory-interpretation question concerns the law’s true meaning and should be corrected on appeal despite forfeiture, but as the Chief Justice explains relying on Singleton v. Wulff, our cases treat consideration of issues not pressed or passed upon below as discretionary and ordinarily inappropriate. Justice Kavanaugh’s citation to Hormel v. Helvering reinforces that any departure from preservation norms is narrow and turns on factors like an adequate record and avoidance of manifest injustice—not a categorical rule triggered by the “pure law” label. Given the lack of certainty that petitioners’ new statutory theory is correct on this record (and the real risk that adversarial development below would have differed), the Tenth Circuit’s “certainty/beyond reasonable doubt” screen represents a permissible exercise of appellate discretion, not a legal error. Nothing in the text of any statute or rule compels an entitlement to reversal on a forfeited theory, so I would affirm.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioners’ strongest contention—that a forfeited statutory-interpretation theory must be reached whenever it presents a “pure question of law”—overreads Hormel and Singleton v. Wulff, which treat such review as discretionary and ordinarily inappropriate absent unusual circumstances. Chief Justice Roberts is right that preservation rules serve legitimacy and the adversarial process: the parties’ litigation choices shape the record and the opponent’s responses, so a late pivot risks sandbagging and distorted development. Justice Kagan’s point about administrability reinforces that the Tenth Circuit’s “certainty/beyond reasonable doubt” screen is a permissible way to channel that discretion rather than a departure from it, especially where correctness is not indisputable on this record. Nothing in text, FRAP practice (as Justice Thomas notes), or our precedents compels an appellate court to reverse on an unpreserved theory simply because it is legal in character.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest point—that a forfeited theory presenting a “pure question of law” must be heard to ensure the correct statutory meaning—runs into the basic structure of our preservation jurisprudence: as the Chief Justice notes, Singleton v. Wulff describes consideration of issues not passed upon below as discretionary and ordinarily inappropriate, not mandatory. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Hormel v. Helvering reinforces that any exception turns on narrow, prudential factors like record adequacy and the need to avert injustice, not the mere “legal” label of the late-raised argument. Under a textualist and precedent-respecting approach, nothing in the Rules or our cases compels converting that discretion into an entitlement, and the Tenth Circuit’s “certainty/beyond reasonable doubt” screen is a permissible way to implement discretion while protecting fair notice and adversarial development. Because the correct disposition is not shown to be certain on this record and the theory was forfeited, I see no basis to reverse.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioners’ strongest claim—that courts of appeals must decide any forfeited “pure question of law” to ensure correct statutory meaning—would effectively convert a prudential preservation doctrine into an entitlement, undermining adversarial testing and inviting strategic sandbagging. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Singleton v. Wulff persuasively frames the inquiry as discretionary and ordinarily inappropriate where the parties’ theories below shaped the record and litigation choices. Justice Kavanaugh’s invocation of Hormel reinforces, for me, that even for legal issues the exception depends on fairness, adequacy of the record, and avoiding injustice, not on a categorical rule; the Tenth Circuit’s “beyond reasonable doubt” certainty screen is a permissible way to channel that discretion. Given the practical consequences for procedural fairness and reliance, I would affirm the enforcement of forfeiture on this record.

John Roberts.reasoning: Appellate preservation rules serve the adversarial process and institutional legitimacy by ensuring issues are tested in the district court and properly briefed on appeal, consistent with ordinary appellate practice reflected in FRAP 28 and our general reluctance to decide issues not passed upon below. Under Singleton v. Wulff, courts of appeals have discretion to consider forfeited issues, but that discretion is properly exercised narrowly, particularly when the late-raised statutory-interpretation theory is not one whose correct resolution is "certain" on the existing record. The Tenth Circuit’s approach in Jarvis and Ave. Capital—declining to entertain new legal arguments unless the proper disposition is beyond reasonable doubt—fits within that discretionary framework and avoids incentivizing sandbagging or piecemeal litigation. Absent a clear, outcome-determinative pure question of law with certain resolution, I would not disturb the court of appeals’ refusal to reach the forfeited theory.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Constitution’s text grants courts appellate jurisdiction, but it does not entitle litigants to reversal on theories never properly presented; preservation rules serve the judicial power’s limited role by ensuring adversarial testing and preventing sandbagging. Under Singleton v. Wulff, 428 U.S. 106 (1976), courts of appeals have discretion—not an obligation—to consider issues not raised below, and that discretion is appropriately exercised sparingly. The Tenth Circuit’s approach in United States v. Jarvis and Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II (considering forfeited pure-law arguments only when the correct disposition is certain/beyond reasonable doubt) is a permissible, orderly method of channeling that discretion consistent with FRAP 28’s briefing requirements and the appellate role. Because petitioners forfeited the statutory-interpretation theory and have no textual entitlement to a discretionary exception, I would affirm the refusal to reach it.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Appellate courts generally do not reverse on theories not pressed below because forfeiture serves adversarial testing, prevents sandbagging, and promotes efficient, orderly adjudication—practical consequences that counsel restraint. Singleton v. Wulff, 428 U.S. 106 (1976), confirms that considering issues not passed upon below is discretionary, not obligatory, and is typically inappropriate absent exceptional circumstances. The Tenth Circuit’s approach—entertaining a forfeited argument only when it presents a pure question of law whose correct resolution is certain—fits comfortably within that discretionary framework and aligns with Jarvis, 499 F.3d 1196, 1202 (10th Cir. 2007), and Schaden, 843 F.3d 876, 886 (10th Cir. 2016). Given the importance of preservation rules and the risk of rewarding late-arising statutory theories, I would affirm the refusal to reach petitioners’ forfeited argument.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I would affirm the court of appeals’ discretion to decline a statutory-interpretation theory first meaningfully advanced after the district court proceedings, because preservation rules protect fairness, adversarial testing, and equal access to justice—especially for parties who litigated the case on the understood issues. Under Singleton v. Wulff, 428 U.S. 106 (1976), an appellate court may consider issues not raised below only in limited circumstances, guided by whether the issue is purely legal and whether the opposing party would be prejudiced; that discretion is not a license for reversal-by-new-theory. The Tenth Circuit’s approach in Jarvis and Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II—requiring that the proper resolution be “certain” or “beyond reasonable doubt” before excusing forfeiture—falls within that discretionary framework and appropriately deters sandbagging and protects reliance interests. Absent clear certainty on the statutory question and with real risk of unfair surprise to the respondent, the forfeiture should be enforced.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Appellate issue-preservation is a judge-made, discretionary doctrine designed to promote fair adversarial testing and efficient, orderly litigation, and Singleton v. Wulff recognizes that while courts of appeals may consider issues not raised below, they ordinarily should not do so absent exceptional circumstances. The Tenth Circuit’s approach—considering forfeited issues only when they present a pure question of law and the correct result is effectively certain (Jarvis; Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II)—fits within that discretionary space and is workably administrable because it channels late-raised arguments into a narrow, predictable exception. Given that a new statutory-interpretation theory can affect factual development, party presentation, and strategic incentives, there is no categorical entitlement to reversal simply because the issue is “legal,” and requiring high confidence before excusing forfeiture appropriately guards against sandbagging and surprise. On this record, the respondent is therefore entitled to affirmance of the court of appeals’ decision to enforce forfeiture rather than reopen the case on a new theory.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Appellate preservation rules serve the adversarial process and respect the proper division of labor between trial and appellate courts; a party that forfeits a statutory-interpretation theory generally may not demand reversal on that new ground. Under United States v. Olano, forfeiture differs from waiver, but relief on unpreserved issues is discretionary and appropriately reserved for circumstances where the error is clear and the outcome-determinative point is beyond reasonable dispute—an approach consistent with the Tenth Circuit’s cases like Jarvis and Avenue Capital. Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 28 reinforces that arguments must be properly presented to be adjudicated, and relaxing forfeiture too freely would invite sandbagging and undermine orderly litigation. Because petitioners did not preserve the new legal theory and its correctness is not shown to be so certain as to justify bypassing the ordinary rules, the Tenth Circuit acted within its discretion in declining to reach it.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: A court of appeals has long-recognized discretion to decline consideration of issues or legal theories not raised below, both to protect the adversarial process and to avoid encouraging sandbagging, and that discretionary, prudential doctrine promotes practical workability and orderly litigation. Under Hormel v. Helvering, 312 U.S. 552 (1941), exceptions for new issues are narrow and generally turn on whether the issue is a pure question of law, the record is adequate, and consideration is necessary to prevent a miscarriage of justice; nothing in Hormel requires an appellate court to reach a forfeited statutory-interpretation theory simply because it is legal in character. The Tenth Circuit’s approach in United States v. Jarvis, 499 F.3d 1196 (10th Cir. 2007), and Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II, L.P. v. Schaden, 843 F.3d 876 (10th Cir. 2016), requiring certainty (“beyond reasonable doubt”) before excusing forfeiture, fits within that permissible discretion and supports judicial restraint and institutional legitimacy by enforcing preservation rules.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Appellate forfeiture is a judge-made, prudential doctrine rooted in the adversarial system, and we have repeatedly emphasized that courts of appeals ordinarily should not decide issues neither pressed nor passed upon below. Singleton v. Wulff, 428 U.S. 106 (1976), frames this as a discretionary choice guided by fairness and the need for adversarial development, and it does not compel review merely because the new theory is styled as a “pure question of law.” The Tenth Circuit’s approach—considering forfeited legal arguments only when the proper disposition is “certain” or “beyond reasonable doubt” (Jarvis; Ave. Capital)—is a permissible way to cabin that discretion to avoid sandbagging and to respect the briefing/preservation norms reflected in FRAP 28 and related preservation principles. On this record, the refusal to reverse on an unpreserved statutory-interpretation theory falls within the court of appeals’ discretion, so I would affirm.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I would affirm the court of appeals’ discretion to decline a statutory-interpretation theory first raised after the district court, because preservation rules protect procedural fairness and ensure adversarial testing rather than surprise on appeal. Singleton v. Wulff, 428 U.S. 106 (1976), recognizes that considering issues not raised below is exceptional and discretionary, not an entitlement, and that appellate courts may insist on full development and fairness to the opposing party. The Tenth Circuit’s approach in Jarvis and Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II—limiting review of forfeited “pure law” arguments to circumstances where the correct resolution is certain or “beyond reasonable doubt”—is a permissible channeling of that discretion to avoid sandbagging and erroneous appellate fact-assumptions. Given the practical consequences for litigants who relied on the issues as framed, I would not require reversal based on a new theory that was not properly preserved and is not indisputably correct on the existing record.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal appellate court may decide a dispositive statutory-interpretation issue that the petitioners did not properly preserve below—treating it as a forfeited (rather than waived) issue—on the theory that it is a “pure question of law” with a “certain” resolution.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal appellate preservation/forfeiture doctrine as applied under the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure and circuit precedent (particularly the Tenth Circuit’s standards for entertaining forfeited issues on appeal); the case appears to arise in a federal labor/employment statutory context (exact underlying statute not identifiable from the provided excerpts).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Flowers Foods and the other petitioners argue that the Tenth Circuit improperly reached and resolved an argument that was not preserved, stretching the “pure matter of law / certain resolution” exception beyond its limits; they contend this undermines party-presentation and issue-preservation rules, creates unfair surprise, and warrants Supreme Court correction (with petitioners’ amici emphasizing administrability and the need to enforce preservation requirements strictly).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Brock argues that the court of appeals properly exercised discretion to consider the forfeited issue because it presented a purely legal question whose correct resolution was clear, and that refusing to consider it would elevate procedural default over correct statutory meaning and just adjudication (with respondent’s amici emphasizing faithful statutory interpretation, worker-protective enforcement, and that discretionary review of forfeited pure legal issues is consistent with appellate practice).

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to emphasize Singleton and Hormel’s recognition of limited appellate discretion to reach forfeited, purely legal issues when the record is adequate and the answer is clear, but that very framing underscores the need for an exceptional, administrable threshold. As Justice Kagan explains, Sineneng-Smith cautions that courts may not recast a case around an unpresented, case-dispositive theory; the Tenth Circuit’s malleable “certain/beyond reasonable doubt” formulation risks turning a safety valve into a routine bypass of preservation and party presentation. Justice Kavanaugh’s point about necessity and avoiding injustice in Hormel reinforces that discretion should be exercised sparingly, and the better minimalist path is to reverse on preservation grounds without deciding the underlying statutory question. That approach protects regularity and legitimacy while leaving room for the merits to be tested in proper adversarial litigation on remand.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that Singleton and Hormel permit discretionary review of a forfeited, purely legal issue when the answer is “certain,” to avoid entrenching statutory error—does not justify what the Tenth Circuit did here, because that discretion is exceptional and cannot swallow the party-presentation and preservation rules that structure Article III adjudication. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize (invoking Sineneng-Smith), allowing panels to relabel a dispositive, unpreserved theory as “certain” invites appellate courts to decide cases as courts of first view and deprives parties of adversarial testing that informs the law’s original public meaning and proper application. Olano’s waiver/forfeiture distinction confirms that forfeiture does not entitle an appellate court to supply and decide a new merits ground simply because it thinks it is right; at most, the remedy is enforcement of ordinary preservation principles or remand for proper litigation. Singleton/Hormel therefore affect my analysis only to the extent they confirm a narrow, necessity-driven safety valve—one the Tenth Circuit’s “beyond reasonable doubt” formulation cannot administer without becoming a general license to bypass preservation.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that Singleton and Hormel recognize limited appellate discretion to consider a forfeited issue of “pure law” on an adequate record to avert obvious error, but that discretion is exceptional and cannot be converted into a case-dispositive license whenever a panel feels confident about statutory meaning. As the Chief Justice stresses, we are a “court of review, not of first view,” and Justice Kagan’s reliance on Sineneng-Smith correctly underscores that party presentation is a structural constraint: deciding a new dispositive statutory theory on appeal—after the parties litigated below on different premises—invites unfair surprise and erodes preservation rules. Justice Thomas’s Olano point reinforces that forfeiture does not authorize appellate courts to supply a fresh merits ground simply because it seems “certain”; the proper course is to enforce preservation (and if necessary remand), not bless an unadministrable “beyond reasonable doubt” shortcut. Under a textualist, consequence-aware approach, predictable preservation rules and fair adversarial testing outweigh the respondent’s accuracy-based argument for appellate correction in the first instance.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right to press that we are generally a “court of review, not first view,” and Sineneng-Smith properly warns against courts driving litigation on theories the parties did not present; that concern meaningfully narrows the discretion I would recognize. But this record still fits the limited Singleton/Hormel category: a purely legal issue, adequate record, and a cabined “beyond reasonable doubt” standard aimed at preventing—not enabling—unfair surprise, so I do not read it as the sort of amici-driven reframing condemned in Sineneng-Smith. Justice Thomas’s Olano point about forfeiture (not waiver) cuts toward allowing discretionary correction in exceptional cases rather than freezing an erroneous statutory rule when no party intentionally relinquished the argument. Under my pragmatic approach, the question is whether enforcing forfeiture here meaningfully improves fairness and legitimacy versus perpetuating clear legal error that predictably burdens workers and other vulnerable litigants; on this record, I do not think the institutional concerns require a categorical reversal.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that Singleton and Hormel preserve some appellate discretion to reach forfeited issues when the question is purely legal and the record is adequate, particularly to avoid entrenching a clear statutory mistake. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, that discretion is exceptional and tied to necessity and fairness; deploying the Tenth Circuit’s “beyond reasonable doubt/certain resolution” language to decide a case-dispositive, unpreserved statutory theory risks converting a safety valve into a routine bypass of preservation rules. Sineneng-Smith matters here even if the posture differs: it underscores that courts should not effectively reframe a case around a new dispositive theory without adversarial testing, and the pragmatic, administrable approach is to enforce forfeiture and, if needed, remand so the issue can be properly litigated. I therefore do not think Sotomayor’s accuracy-based argument overcomes the institutional and party-presentation costs of affirming this kind of appellate innovation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to stress Singleton and Hormel: they recognize some appellate discretion to consider a forfeited, purely legal issue when the record is adequate and the answer is clear. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, that safety valve cannot be converted into a general merits shortcut without collapsing party-presentation and preservation norms and inviting the kind of appellate case-recasting Sineneng-Smith condemns. Justice Thomas’s point underscores the structural nature of these constraints: forfeiture may leave room for discretion, but only in truly exceptional circumstances tethered to necessity and administrable standards, not a panel’s confidence in statutory meaning. The proper course is to vacate and remand for ordinary preservation principles rather than endorse the Tenth Circuit’s unworkable “certain/beyond reasonable doubt” pathway to decide a case-dispositive issue in the first instance on appeal.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to invoke Singleton and Hormel for the proposition that courts of appeals retain some discretion to reach forfeited issues when the question is purely legal and the answer is clear, but that discretion is exceptional and tied to necessity and fairness—not a warrant to decide a case-dispositive statutory theory newly minted on appeal. Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s “court of review, not first view” and Sineneng-Smith concerns sharpen why the Tenth Circuit’s “beyond reasonable doubt/certain resolution” label is not self-policing: it invites panels to bypass preservation whenever they feel confident, undermining party presentation and administrable rules. Even under Sotomayor’s framing, the safer institutional course is to enforce forfeiture here (or remand) rather than bless a merits ruling rendered without full adversarial testing below. Olano’s waiver/forfeiture distinction (as Justice Thomas notes) confirms discretion exists, but it does not justify converting forfeiture into an appellate license to redesign the case.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that Singleton and Hormel recognize some appellate discretion to consider forfeited issues, especially when the question is purely legal and the record is adequate. But as Justice Kagan emphasizes via Sineneng-Smith, that discretion is bounded by party presentation; it cannot be used to reframe a case around a new, case-dispositive statutory theory the parties did not litigate below, particularly where the absence of preservation itself shapes what was argued and what evidence (if any) was developed. Justice Roberts’s concern about administrability resonates: the Tenth Circuit’s “beyond reasonable doubt/certain resolution” standard is too malleable to prevent routine bypass of forfeiture, and Singleton’s exception is meant to be rare and fairness-tethered, not a merits shortcut whenever a panel feels confident. The proper course is to enforce preservation (with remand if necessary) rather than bless an approach that predictably erodes regular order and incentivizes strategic omission.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s accuracy-based defense—rooted in Singleton and Hormel—rightly highlights that appellate courts retain some discretion to reach forfeited pure legal issues to avoid locking in clear statutory error, including in worker-protection contexts. But as Justice Kagan underscores with Sineneng-Smith, and as the Chief Justice notes, the problem here is procedural fairness: the court of appeals used a “certain resolution/beyond reasonable doubt” label to decide a dispositive theory without the adversarial development that preservation rules are designed to ensure, inviting one-sided statutory analysis and sandbagging incentives. Singleton’s discretion is exceptional and fairness-tethered; it does not justify transforming appellate confidence into a routine bypass of party presentation, particularly where the record and briefing posture were shaped by the forfeiture. The pragmatic remedy is vacatur and remand so the statutory question can be litigated with notice and a proper record, rather than blessing an unadministrable shortcut.

John Roberts.reasoning: Ordinarily we are “a court of review, not of first view,” and questions not properly presented below are forfeited absent exceptional circumstances. Singleton v. Wulff, 428 U.S. 106 (1976), recognizes only limited appellate discretion to reach a new issue, and that discretion must be exercised narrowly to protect party presentation and the orderly operation of preservation rules. The Tenth Circuit’s “pure question of law”/“certain resolution” exception, as articulated in Jarvis and Avenue Capital, cannot justify deciding a dispositive statutory-interpretation question when the “proper legal disposition” is not beyond reasonable doubt and the parties lacked a fair opportunity to develop the issue below. Reversing on narrow grounds to enforce preservation doctrine best serves institutional legitimacy and administrable appellate practice without opining on the underlying statutory merits.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Appellate review in our system is generally limited to issues properly presented and preserved by the parties, and a court of appeals exceeds its proper role when it reaches out to decide a dispositive statutory-interpretation question that was not preserved below merely by labeling it a “pure question of law.” Under United States v. Olano, forfeiture (failure to timely assert a right) is distinct from waiver (intentional relinquishment), and unpreserved issues are ordinarily reviewed—if at all—only under constrained standards rather than as an alternative merits ground that supplants the party-presentation and preservation rules. Allowing a broad “certain resolution” exception invites appellate courts to revise the case on their own initiative, undermining orderly procedure embodied in the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure and eroding the limited, adjudicative judicial role. The Tenth Circuit’s approach, as described, stretches any discretionary exception beyond administrable bounds and warrants correction.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: A court of appeals should not decide a dispositive statutory-interpretation theory that the party failed to preserve below merely by labeling it a “pure question of law” with a “certain” answer, because that approach erodes party-presentation and preservation rules and invites unfair surprise. Under United States v. Olano, forfeiture is distinct from waiver, and while forfeited issues may sometimes be reviewed, appellate discretion is limited and must be exercised with caution—especially when the issue is case-dispositive and the record and adversarial testing below were shaped by the parties’ omissions. The Tenth Circuit’s permissive “pure law/certain resolution” exception, as reflected in cases like Jarvis, cannot be allowed to swallow preservation requirements by routinely reaching unpreserved statutory arguments. Practical consequences also counsel restraint: relaxing preservation predictably incentivizes sandbagging and undermines orderly litigation and the finality of district-court proceedings.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Appellate courts retain discretion to consider forfeited (not waived) issues in exceptional circumstances, and Singleton v. Wulff recognizes that discretion particularly where the issue is a “pure question of law” and the record is adequate. The Tenth Circuit’s own standards in United States v. Jarvis and Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II allow review when the legal answer is “certain” or “beyond reasonable doubt,” which mitigates unfair surprise and protects accuracy in statutory interpretation. Where the dispositive question is purely legal and its correct resolution is clear, refusing to address it can entrench an erroneous construction that disproportionately harms vulnerable parties (here, workers’ ability to vindicate statutory rights) without advancing any substantial fairness interest. Given the forfeiture posture and the court’s limited, discretionary use of this narrow exception, I would affirm the permissibility of reaching the issue in these circumstances.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: An appellate court’s discretion to consider forfeited issues is real, but it is bounded by the party-presentation principle and by the need for administrable preservation rules. Under United States v. Sineneng-Smith, a court of appeals should not decide a dispositive statutory-interpretation theory that the parties did not properly present, especially where doing so risks unfair surprise and turns the “pure question of law/certain resolution” exception into a broad license to bypass forfeiture. The Tenth Circuit’s own precedents (e.g., Jarvis and Avenue Capital Management II) treat review of forfeited issues as exceptional and case-specific; using that exception to resolve a case-dispositive statutory meaning question absent proper preservation undermines workability and the coherent operation of adversarial litigation and FRAP-based preservation norms. The better course is to enforce forfeiture here and remand if necessary for the issue to be properly litigated rather than having the appellate court supply a new, dispositive theory on its own.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Appellate courts generally sit to review questions the parties have properly presented and preserved, and stretching a discretionary “pure question of law/certain resolution” exception to decide a dispositive, unpreserved statutory-interpretation theory risks turning courts into roving commissions rather than neutral arbiters. That move undermines party presentation and preservation principles emphasized by this Court in United States v. Sineneng-Smith, which cautions that courts may not recast a case around issues the parties did not properly litigate. Whatever discretion exists to consider forfeited issues should be exercised sparingly and with clear administrable limits; otherwise it erodes the separation-of-powers values served by procedural rules and invites unpredictability. Because the Tenth Circuit treated an unpreserved, case-dispositive statutory issue as forfeited and then resolved it on its own “certain” view of the law, I would vacate and remand for application of ordinary preservation principles.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Issue-preservation principles and the party-presentation rule generally constrain appellate courts from deciding unpreserved statutory-interpretation theories, and discretionary departures should remain narrow to protect fairness and administrability. Although Hormel v. Helvering, 312 U.S. 552 (1941), recognizes limited discretion to entertain issues not raised below, it ties that discretion to avoiding injustice and practical necessity—not to routine correction of forfeited arguments whenever a panel deems the answer “certain.” The Tenth Circuit’s own formulations in United States v. Jarvis, 499 F.3d 1196 (10th Cir. 2007), and Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II, L.P. v. Schaden, 843 F.3d 876 (10th Cir.), underscore that even “pure” legal issues should not be considered unless the correct disposition is beyond reasonable doubt; expanding that exception risks undermining workability and incentives to preserve issues in the district court. On these premises, the court of appeals overstepped by resolving a dispositive statutory question that petitioners did not properly preserve.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Issue-preservation is a central feature of the adversarial system and appellate review, and an appellate court should not decide a dispositive statutory-interpretation question that a party failed to raise below absent a disciplined, consistently applied exception. Under United States v. Olano, the line between waiver and forfeiture matters: forfeiture may permit review only under constrained standards, and courts should be wary of recasting nonpreservation as a license to reach new theories simply because they are labeled “pure questions of law.” The Tenth Circuit’s own precedent (Jarvis and Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II) underscores that even “pure” legal issues should be considered only when the correct outcome is “certain” or “beyond reasonable doubt,” a demanding threshold that is not met when the question is contested, fact-bound in application, or effectively one of first impression. Allowing routine merits resolution of forfeited statutory arguments risks undermining methodological consistency, party presentation, and fair notice, so I would reverse and enforce the preservation limits more strictly.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I would reverse because the court of appeals’ decision to resolve a dispositive statutory-interpretation theory that was not properly preserved below undermines party presentation and basic procedural fairness, risking unfair surprise and a one-sided record. Under Singleton v. Wulff, 428 U.S. 106 (1976), appellate consideration of issues not raised is discretionary and generally inappropriate where it would prejudice the opposing party or where the record was not developed with that issue in mind; the asserted “pure question of law” label cannot substitute for those fairness constraints. The Tenth Circuit’s “certain resolution” rationale (as reflected in cases like Jarvis and Ave. Cap. Mgmt.) should be applied narrowly, and not to decide the case on a forfeited ground when the parties lacked a fair opportunity to litigate it in the district court. A remand (or refusal to consider the forfeited argument) better serves administrability and procedural regularity while still permitting correct statutory interpretation through proper presentation.
